title: 10 Things: Common Problems With Do Now Activities
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: Tom Sherrington catalogues ten common problems with Do Now lesson-starter activities (DNAs), arguing that while they reliably achieve a calm, ordered start to lessons, they frequently fail as learning tools - especially for less confident students. His central diagnosis is that DNAs are usually asked to do three different jobs at once - settle behaviour, consolidate prior learning, and function as retrieval-practice testing - and trying to satisfy all three in one silent routine produces predictable failure points. He works through specific mechanisms: too many questions for the time available, insufficiently consolidatory content that doesn't function as a genuine warm-up, students unable to self-check efficiently, and - what he treats as the most damaging gap - insufficient time spent identifying and addressing wrong answers, leaving teachers to simply hope that hearing the correct answer functions as re-teaching. He also flags structural design problems: DNAs that awkwardly interrupt rather than precede the lesson's actual topic, and topic-mixing grids so wide-ranging that weaker students face recall questions on material they had no warning would resurface, which he calls a total train wreck for the students least able to cope with it.
points: Sherrington's core diagnosis is that Do Now activities conflate three distinct purposes - behaviour settling, consolidation warm-up, and retrieval testing - into one silent routine, and the conflation is what causes most of the practical failures.
He argues the standard 10-questions-in-silence format overloads weaker students specifically, since it assumes a fluency they may not have and leaves them starting the lesson already feeling behind.

Sherrington singles out the failure to check wrong answers as the most consequential gap: without identifying who got what wrong, teachers default to hoping the correct answer alone will re-teach the content, which he argues is rarely sufficient.

His complaint about overly wide topic mixes spanning weeks of content names a specific and common retrieval-practice failure mode where students face recall questions on material they were never warned would resurface.
quotes: My honest evaluation of this very common practise is mixed: the Do Now routine usually achieves the goal of creating a calm lesson start but, in terms of learning, quite a lot of the time it doesn’t work very well at all, especially for the least confident students.

Quite often too many questions are set to be completed in the time, to go over the answers and to re-teach where problems arise. It’s over-cooked. 10 questions is only workable if you can do them all relatively easily

A warm-up ought be positive, affirming and largely consolidatory – like a band or choir warming up playing one of their familiar songs to get everyone in the groove with some mental rehearsal of familiar material.

Often, when time is pressing, the bit that is missed is the part when you check for wrong answers, areas of confusion, concerns, questions- so students who get quite a few items wrong are not identified to the teacher.

There’s just a hope that telling them the answer IS the reteach -when obviously that’s often far from sufficient. This means that you can bet the same students will get the same DNA questions wrong again next time
It's just so common for these wide topic range starter to be a total train wreck for the weakest students.
